preamble: Raising of the open-mid front [ɛ] to near-close [ɪ]. Its best-known case is the pin–pen merger of Southern American English, a conditioned merger of /ɛ/ with /ɪ/ before the nasals /m n ŋ/, so that pen sounds like pin and hem like him. Written responses of American Civil War veterans from Tennessee and linguistic-atlas data show the merger was rare before 1860 and reached 90% in the mid-20th century. Raising of /ɛ/ to /ɪ/ was formerly widespread in Irish English and is now mostly limited to the pre-nasal position in Southern and South-West Irish English.

examples.note: Other merged pairs include Ben–bin, den–din, gem–gym and Ken–kin, all with [ɪ]; the merger is absent from Savannah, Miami and New Orleans.

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Phonological history of English close front vowels. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonological_history_of_English_close_front_vowels
